rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Species epithets such as Abū al-Ḥārith and Thaʿāla are conventional proper forms shared by every member of a kind, unlike an individual proper name.
rows.anchor: فكل هذا يجرى خبره مجرى خبر عبد الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pointing to Abū al-Ḥārith or Thaʿāla identifies a lion or fox as a kind, not one previously identified animal.
rows.anchor: هذا أبو الحارث أو هذا ثعالة أنك تريد هذا الأسد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A name such as Zayd singles out an individual already known by distinguishing features or a defining report.
rows.anchor: فكأنك إذا قلت هذا زيد قلت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common noun rajul can mean a particular whole man or any male human; Zayd removes that ambiguity by naming one individual.
rows.anchor: كل ذكر تكلم ومشى على رجلين فهو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wild animals did not need individual names because they were not continuously present or recognizable by retained appearance; people individually named horses, camels, sheep, and dogs kept among them.
rows.anchor: ليست بأشياء ثابتة مقيمة مع الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Names for particular species and subtypes, including Ibn Qitra and Banāt Awbar, function as definite labels for a recognized kind, unlike generic animal nouns that can be definite or indefinite.
rows.anchor: اختصت العرب لكل ضرب من هذه الضروب اسما

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr treats compounds such as Ibn ʿArs as definite because an article cannot be added to their second element; Yūnus transmitted his view.
rows.anchor: وهو قول أبى عمرو حدثنا به يونس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For Ibn Qitra and Ḥimār Qubbān, the lack of declension in the element after the first compound element also signals definiteness.
rows.anchor: وما أشبههما فيدلك على معرفتهن ترك

rows.speaker: بعض العرب
rows.claim: Some Arabs say hādhā Ibn ʿArs muqbil with muqbil nominative; Sībawayh gives two possible grammatical analyses.
rows.anchor: زعموا أن بعض العرب يقول هذا ابن عرس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One analysis makes muqbil a direct predicate, as in hādhā Zaydun muqbil; the other treats the following description as indefinite and the compound as attached to an indefinite phrase.
rows.anchor: فوجه مثل هذا زيد مقبل ووجه على أنه جعل ما بعده نكرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second analysis is needed because an indefinite noun cannot be annexed to a definite one; the phrase is instead made indefinite.
rows.anchor: لأنه لا يكون الاسم نكرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Labūn and Ibn Makhāḍ are indefinite because they accept the definite article.
rows.anchor: وأما ابن لبون وابن مخاض فنكرة لأنها تدخلها الألف واللام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sībawayh cites Jarīr’s Ibn al-Labūn, Abū ʿAṭāʾ’s Banāt al-Māʾ, and al-Razdaq’s Ibn al-Makhāḍ as article-bearing forms, showing these compounds are indefinite without the article.
rows.anchor: ابن اللبون إذا ما لز فى قرن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhū al-Rumma’s articleless Ibn Māʾ example shows that removing the article leaves the phrase indefinite.
rows.anchor: على قمة الرأس ابن ماء محلق

rows.speaker: ناس
rows.claim: Some claim every Ibn Afʿal compound is definite because it is indeclinable; Sībawayh rejects this, since Afʿal adjectives can be indefinite and indeclinable.
rows.anchor: وقال ناس كل ابن أفعل معرفة لأنه لا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sībawayh adduces Dhū al-Rumma’s awlād aḥqab as a poetic example of an indefinite Afʿal form.
rows.anchor: كأنا على أولاد أحقب لاحها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A masculine given a feminine name of four or more letters is diptote because the naming departs from the form originally suited to masculine referents, like a foreign name.
rows.anchor: كل مذكر سميته بمؤنث على أربعة أحرف فصاعدا لم ينصرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAnāq, ʿAqrab, ʿAqāb, and ʿAnkabūt exemplify feminine names that make a masculine bearer diptote.
rows.anchor: فمن ذلك عناق وعقرب وعقاب وعنكبوت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dh irāʿ is declinable as a masculine name because it became common and established for men, and it can describe a masculine noun such as thawb.
rows.anchor: وسألته عن ذراع فقال ذراع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preferred treatment of Kurāʿ is diptote; declension by analogy with Dh irāʿ is attested but is the weaker analysis.
rows.anchor: وأما كراع فإن الوجه ترك الصرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A man named Thumānī or Thalāth is diptote because each is a feminine numeral form.
rows.anchor: لم تصرفه لأن ثماني ~~اسم لمؤنث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The diminutive Ḥubayr from Ḥubārā remains diptote because the original name is feminine even after the diminutive element is removed.
rows.anchor: فالياء إذا ذهبت فإنما هي مؤنثة كعنيق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Masculine names from feminine adjectives such as Ḥāʾiḍ, Ṭāmiṯ, and Mutʾim are declinable because those forms are masculine in morphology while describing females.
rows.anchor: إذا سميت المذكر بصفة المؤنث صرفته

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl explains that faʿūl and mifʿāl lack feminine marking because they entered usage as masculine forms that can describe feminine referents.
rows.anchor: وزعم الخليل أن فعولا ومفعالا إنما امتنعتا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Names such as Qāʿid, Ḍārib, and ʿĀqir remain declinable when intended as feminine descriptions, by analogy with masculine forms used for females.
rows.anchor: فلو لم تصرف حائضا لم تصرف رجلا يسمى قاعدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some feminine forms, including Yafʿa and Rabʿa, can describe either males or females, unlike forms restricted to feminine referents.
rows.anchor: ومما جاء مؤنثا صفة تقع للمذكر والمؤنث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Feminine-only adjectives used of masculine names are understood as originally describing a thing, person, or eye.
rows.anchor: المؤنث لا يقع إلا لمذكر وصفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wind words such as Ḥarūr, Shimāl, Janūb, and Samūm are usually adjectives in Arab usage, so a man named by one is declinable.
rows.anchor: لأنها صفات في أكثر كلام العرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Aʿshā’s rīḥan dabūran line supports describing feminine rīḥ with the masculine-form word dabūr.
rows.anchor: صادف بالليل ريحا دبورا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wind words are rarely treated as nouns; the cited poetry supplies such noun-like examples, which are then indeclinable when used as men’s names.
rows.anchor: فمن جعلها أسماء لم يصرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Established feminine names such as Suʿād, Zaynab, and Jayʾal are diptote, while masculine nouns used as men’s names, such as Rabāb and Dalāl, are declinable.
rows.anchor: وإذا سميت رجلا بسعاد أو زينب أو جيأل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Names such as Khurūq, Kilāb, and Jimāl are declinable because these forms can denote masculine groups and are not exclusive feminine names.
rows.anchor: واعلم أنك إذا سميت رجلا خروقا أو كلابا أو جمالا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAnūq is declinable because its feminine ending is the masculine plural pattern; it differs from ʿAnāq, a feminine species name.
rows.anchor: فإن قلت ما تقول في رجل يسمى بعنوق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nisāʾ is declinable as a masculine name because it is the plural of Niswah, like other masculine-plural forms.
rows.anchor: وكذلك رجل يسمى نساء لأنها جمع نسوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭāghūt is one feminine noun that can refer collectively to a group; 39:17 illustrates this with the feminine pronoun ʿabudūhā.
rows.anchor: والذين اجتنبوا الطاغوت ~~أن يعبدوها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A feminine collective with no singular, such as Ibil or Ghanam, is treated like a feminine singular and is diptote when used as a masculine name.
rows.anchor: نحو ابل وغنم لأنه ليس له واحد

rows.speaker: يونس
rows.claim: Yūnus reports that names for letters and other invariable words vary in grammatical gender: some Arabs treat them as feminine and others as masculine.
rows.anchor: ويؤنث زعم ذلك يونس وأنشدنا

rows.speaker: الراجز
rows.claim: The rajaz poet uses Kāf, Mīm, and Sīn with a masculine adjective, ṭāsima.
rows.anchor: كافا وميمين وسينا طاسما

rows.speaker: الراعي
rows.claim: Al-Rāʿī uses Kāf and Mīm with a feminine verb, showing the alternative feminine agreement.
rows.anchor: كما بينت كاف تلوح وميمها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When these items are pronounced with a vowel in context, fatḥ is preferred because they behave like verbs such as kāna.
rows.anchor: أواخرهما بالفتح لأنهما بمنزلة الأفعال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A letter name used for the letter itself is declinable; when it names a word, the form follows the gender language chosen by the speaker.
rows.anchor: واحدا من الحرفين اسما للحرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Turning a particle into a name requires changing its former grammatical state, just as naming from a verb changes it into a noun.
rows.anchor: ولا بد لكل واحد من الحرفين إذا جعلته اسما

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl distinguishes ʾan and ʾin: ʾan is noun-like and can represent a verbal noun, while ʾin is verb-like.
rows.anchor: أن غير إن إن كالفعل أن كالاسم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Law and ʾAw end in sukūn; when made names they follow Layt and ʾIn in gender and declension, but their final wāw is doubled.
rows.anchor: ساكنتا الأواخر لأن قبل آخر كل واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Zubayd’s verse shows the named forms Laytā and Lawā with lengthened final consonants.
rows.anchor: ليت شعري وأين مني ليت

rows.speaker: العرب
rows.claim: Some Arabs pronounce Law as Lawʾ, analogous to al-naʾūr, to avoid the excessive loss that inflection would cause to a wāw preceded by fatḥ.
rows.anchor: لوء وإنما دعاهم إلى تثقيل لو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The names Hū and Hī double their final wāw or yāʾ when used as names, since those endings are not ordinary inflectional endings.
rows.anchor: فمما جاء فيه الواو وقبله مضموم هو

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl analyzes Dhū as having the basic pattern faʿl with fatḥ on dhāl, supported by its forms Dhawā and Dhawū.
rows.anchor: وكان الخليل يقول هذا ذو بفتح الذال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kay and Fī lengthen their final yāʾ because Arabic has no ordinary word ending in yāʾ preceded by fatḥ; Fī would also be too reduced if nunated.
rows.anchor: وأما كي فتثقل ياؤها لأنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lā and Fī are extended in both declinable and diptote naming, masculine and feminine, to prevent names from collapsing to one letter in connected speech.
rows.anchor: التأنيث والتذكير ككي ولو وقصتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When Dhā or Mā becomes a name, it is lengthened; as a feminine name it is diptote because the original forms are masculine.
rows.anchor: وإذا صارت ذا اسما أو ما مدت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fū is replaced by Famm when isolated because Arabs already changed its final wāw to mīm to fit a familiar noun pattern; otherwise it would be derived from Fūh.
rows.anchor: وسألته عن رجل اسمه فو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Letter names such as Bāʾ, Tāʾ, and Fāʾ are lengthened when made names; as names for words they remain indefinite, as shown by their accepting the article.
rows.anchor: وأما البا والتا والثا واليا والحا والخا والرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alphabet names used for words resemble indefinite Ibn Makhāḍ and Ibn Labūn, unlike fixed definite species names such as Sām Abras and Umm Ḥubayn.
rows.anchor: يدلك على أنهن نكرة إذا لم يكن فيهن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In spelling, alphabet letters are shortened and left unvowelled because they are pauses and sounds, not lexical names; Qāf, Ṣād, and Dāl show the pause form.
rows.anchor: تهجيت مقصورة لأنها ليست بأسماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pronouncing spelled letters is like making sounds and stopping, unlike wāḥid ithnān, where wāḥid is a fully inflected noun.
rows.anchor: وليست هذه الحروف مما يدرج ليس أصلها الإدراج

rows.speaker: العرب
rows.claim: A trusted informant heard speakers transfer the hamza of arbaʿa onto the preceding hāʾ in thalātha arbaʿa; the hāʾ stays fixed like a consonant in connected speech.
rows.anchor: ثلاثة أربعة طرح همزة أربعة على الهاء

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl says spelled letter sequences retain their alphabet names, as in lām alif; a poetic line attests writing that sequence.
rows.anchor: تكتبان في الطريق لام ألف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zāy has two spelling pronunciations: one patterned like Kay, and the more common one Zāy, patterned like Wāw.
rows.anchor: وأما زاي ففيها لغتان فمنهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Particles such as Umm, Man, ʾIn, and Mudh do not change when named because they resemble short nouns such as Yad and Dam.
rows.anchor: ومذ في لغة من جر وأن وعن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Naʿam and Biʾs remain unchanged because they are verbs; verbs are grammatically masculine and are not treated as ordinary names of words.
rows.anchor: لأنهن أفعال والأفعال على

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Any alphabet letter made a name for a letter, a word, or something else follows the naming pattern of Lā, as in Bāʾ.
rows.anchor: واعلم أنك إذا جعلت حرفا من حروف المعجم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A suffixed pronoun yāʾ, whether genitive or accusative, keeps its vowel because it is weak and hidden rather than a case ending.
rows.anchor: هذا غلاميه وجاء من بعديه وإنه ضربنيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Speakers who make the yāʾ quiescent do not add hāʾ in pause, since nothing has been deleted from the connected form.
rows.anchor: وأما من رأى أن يسكن الياء

rows.speaker: العرب
rows.claim: Some forms add hāʾ after Hī and Hū in pause because their final yāʾ and wāw are not inflectional endings and are not left fully quiescent.
rows.anchor: وقالوا هيه وهم يريدون هي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same pause hāʾ appears in forms such as khudh-hu bi-ḥukmika; speakers who omit it with the earlier pronouns omit it here too.
rows.anchor: ومثل ذلك قولهم خذه بحكمكه وجميع هذا في الوصل

rows.speaker: العرب
rows.claim: Hāʾ and alif can both clarify a weak ending in pause: ḥayhalā becomes ḥayhal bi-ʿAmr in connection, though ḥayhal may also remain.
rows.anchor: قالوا حيهل بعمر وإن شئت قلت حيهل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Anā retains final alif in pause and has no hāʾ variant; its short, hidden nūn and status as a minimal independent word distinguish it from Hū.
rows.anchor: ولا يكون في الوقف في أنا إلا الألف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No pause hāʾ is added to a fully inflected ending such as aḥmar, whose final changes for case and accepts the article.
rows.anchor: وأما أحمر ونحوه إذا قلت رأيت أحمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verbs such as ẓanna and ḍaraba likewise take no pause hāʾ because their final consonants vary with inflection.
rows.anchor: لما كانت اللام قد تصرف حتى يدخلها الرفع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Interrogative particles clipped from mā, such as ʿalāma, fīma, lima, bima, and ḥattāma, preferably take hāʾ in pause because deletion leaves a weak ending.
rows.anchor: وأما قولهم علامه وفيمه ولمه وبمه وحتامه

rows.speaker: العرب
rows.claim: Some speakers omit pause hāʾ from clipped mā forms, by analogy with ʾikhsha; ʾIn is not a parallel because nothing was deleted from it.
rows.anchor: كما قالوا اخش وليس هذه مثل إن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In majīʾ ma jiʾta and mithl ma anta, pause hāʾ is obligatory because majīʾ and mithl are independent nouns; unlike the clipped particles, the first element is a noun.
rows.anchor: وأما قولهم مجيء م جئت ومثل م أنت

rows.speaker: العرب
rows.claim: A pause hāʾ may follow the weak alif in hāʾulāʾ and hahunā for clarity; it is avoided with inflected nouns such as afʿā and aʿmā, where it could be confused with possessive hāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقد لحقت هذه الهاءات بعد الألف في الوقف

rows.speaker: العرب
rows.claim: Hāʾ is not attached after a preceding sukūn; many Arabs also omit it in pause when the ending is clear from context.
rows.anchor: هم لا يتبعون الهاء ساكنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Vocatives and lament forms add hāʾ after long alif, wāw, or yāʾ in pause to sustain and clarify the call, then drop it in connected speech.
rows.anchor: والألف والياء والواو في الندبة
